findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The MTFS does not take account of the impact of Local Government Reorganisation.
findings.detail: The paper says the projected end date of the strategy may extend beyond the potential start date for any new unitary authority. It does not quantify the effect of reorganisation on the forecasts.
findings.matters: A forecast that does not reflect a known structural change in the council's own status is a gap that finance directors across the county area will need to address in their own plans.
findings.figures: None given in the paper for this point
findings.quote: The MTFS has not taken any account of the impact of LGR.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The paper states that Core Spending Power will fall in real terms across the transitional period and beyond.
findings.detail: The paper shows Revenue Support Grant falling from £4,281k in 2026/27 to £3,854k in 2027/28 and £3,400k in 2028/29. It also says the Fair Funding Review and business rates reset present considerable risk to grant funding.
findings.matters: A real-terms fall in Core Spending Power is the headline measure of government support that peer councils and lenders compare when assessing council funding.
findings.quote: Although some transitional arrangements were applied to limit the impact, the Council’s Core Spending Power (CSP) will fall in real terms across the transitional period and beyond.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The Nottinghamshire Business Rates Pool was dissolved at the end of 2025/26, and the councils will not pool again in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The Nottinghamshire Finance Officers Association agreed the dissolution after reviewing that the risks now outweighed any rewards following the business rates reset. The paper says the pool had retained over £74m of growth in earlier years.
findings.matters: Leaving a business rates pool removes a source of retained growth, and other councils considering the same reset will weigh the same risk against the reward.
findings.figures: Over £74m of growth retained locally by the pool in earlier years; £2.971m Baseline Funding Level for Broxtowe
findings.quote: As such, the NFOA agreed to dissolve the Nottinghamshire Business Rates Pool at the end of 2025/26 and revoke the intention to pool again in 2026/27 with MHCLG.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: Broxtowe received £739k of Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27, with no commitment to extend it into 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper describes the grant as a one-off allocation that gave temporary protection to Core Spending Power. It records that the loss of this grant presents a real funding risk, and the MTFS assumes it ends after 2026/27.
findings.matters: A one-off grant that makes up part of a council's 2026/27 funding and is not assumed to continue is a funding cliff that other councils with similar protections will also face.
findings.figures: £739k Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27; nil in 2027/28 onwards in the MTFS
findings.quote: This late change saw Broxtowe receive £739k in Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27. There is currently no commitment to extend this grant into 2027/28 and beyond

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: Broxtowe secured £21.1m of Towns Deal funding for development projects in Stapleford and a £16.5m grant for the Kimberley Means Business regeneration project.
findings.detail: The paper says these grants have boosted the General Fund capital programme alongside the Bramcote scheme. It also notes the council is seeking further funding through the East Midlands County Combined Authority.
findings.matters: Externally funded regeneration grants reduce the council's reliance on borrowing and capital receipts, which peers and lenders will want to see in the funding mix.
findings.figures: £21.1m Towns Deal funding for Stapleford; £16.5m grant for Kimberley Means Business
findings.quote: The Council was successful in bidding for the Government’s Towns Deal funding to regenerate Stapleford, with £21.1m being secured for development projects in Stapleford.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The paper reports that delivery of the capital programme is under pressure and that reserve schemes cannot proceed for lack of a funding source.
findings.detail: The paper lists delays from internal resource shortages, contractor shortages, supply chain issues and construction price inflation. It also says a lack of capital receipts and unrestricted grants is limiting progress on reserve schemes, particularly given the Bramcote commitment.
findings.matters: A capital programme with approved schemes waiting on funding is a common pressure, and the paper's causes are useful for finance officers comparing delivery problems across councils.
findings.figures: None given in the paper for this point
findings.quote: This continues to limit progress with delivering reserve schemes in the capital programme which have been unable to proceed at present due to the lack of a source of funds.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: Financing the Bramcote Leisure Centre with £18m of prudential borrowing is estimated to cost around £1.25m per annum in capital financing.
findings.detail: The paper says the full revenue pressure will arise after completion from 2028/29, with interest costs during the build depending on borrowing requirements. A 1% change in interest rates is estimated to change annual borrowing costs by £180k.
findings.matters: The annual revenue cost of prudential borrowing, and its sensitivity to rates, is the figure a finance director must absorb in the base budget and a lender will test against the council's debt position.
findings.figures: £18m prudential borrowing; around £1.25m per annum; £180k per 1% change in interest rates
findings.quote: The revenue implications of the capital financing costs of the scheme, assuming £18m of prudential borrowing is required, is around £1.25m per annum.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The new replacement Bramcote Leisure Centre has updated estimated construction costs of £22.5m.
findings.detail: The paper records around £1.0m of costs already committed and says the scheme is funded from General Fund capital receipts, capital grants, external contributions including potential Section 106 allocations, and prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: A large leisure scheme funded partly by prudential borrowing is the kind of capital commitment a lender or peer finance officer will want to track against cost and funding.
findings.figures: £22.5m estimated construction cost; around £1.0m already committed
findings.quote: A further report to Cabinet on 2 June 2026, provided updated estimated capital costs for the construction of the new leisure centre at £22.5m, including around £1.0m of costs already committed

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The General Fund establishment is forecast to achieve its £800.000 turnover target in 2026/27, and the target is proposed to rise to £900,000.
findings.detail: The paper says the forecast turnover equals 4.9% of the General Fund salary budget. The increase is justified by pay inflation and growth in the establishment.
findings.matters: A turnover target that is forecast to be met, and then raised, is a staffing lever other finance directors use to close gaps, and the rising target adds to the savings the budget depends on.
findings.figures: £800.000 turnover target (2026/27), 4.9% of GF salary budget; proposed increase to £900,000
findings.quote: The General Fund (GF) establishment budget is forecast to achieve the £800.000 turnover target in 2026/27 (4.9% of GF salary budget).

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The management fee paid to Liberty Leisure Limited is proposed to fall from £200,000 to £100,000 in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper links the reduction to efficiency savings and income levels at Liberty Leisure Limited, which held general reserves of £445,129 at 31 March 2026. The full fee was not taken in 2025/26, and part of it was retained by the council in a Leisure Development Reserve.
findings.matters: Reducing a council-owned leisure company's fee shifts the cost between the council and its subsidiary, which other councils running similar arrangements will recognise.
findings.figures: £200,000 current annual management fee; £100,000 proposed for 2027/28; £445,129 LLL general reserves at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: It is proposed to reduce the management fee to £100,000 in 2027/28 to reflects the efficiency savings and income levels being achieved by LLL

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The 2027/28 Business Strategy identifies £950,000 of additional savings and income.
findings.detail: The total is made up of proposals including £250,000 of rental and property income, £100,000 from the staffing efficiency target and £200,000 of other council tax and trade waste changes. The paper notes that several proposals still need detailed engagement during budget setting.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the scale of identified savings against the forecast gap, and peers can see which income streams another council is relying on.
findings.figures: £950,000 total additional savings and income for 2027/28
findings.quote: Total 2027/28 additional savings and income identified £950,000

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The MTFS shows a planned deficit to be met from the General Fund of £895k in 2026/27, rising to £1,807k in 2027/28 and £2,417k in 2030/31.
findings.detail: The paper describes budget pressures on the 2027/28 budget, including pay awards, employer National Insurance and pension contributions, and energy and fuel prices. Movements from earmarked reserves are shown as offsets against the deficit.
findings.matters: A planned deficit that grows each year and is met from reserves is the trajectory a finance director must close or explain, and lenders track it as a measure of structural balance.
findings.quote: There continues to be significant budget pressures highlighted that will impact on the Council’s 2027/28 budget.

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: Available reserves are projected to fall below the £1,500k minimum balance in 2028/29, reaching £(431k) in that year.
findings.detail: The paper shows available reserves at £3,345k in 2026/27 and £1,538k in 2027/28. The table marks years below the minimum balance in bold, and the paper's own note refers to that marking.
findings.matters: Falling below a stated minimum reserve is a threshold a finance director must report on, and peers can compare the timing against their own minimum balances.
findings.quote: (Figures in bold - below minimum balance)

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The MTFS projects General Fund closing balances of £4,845k at the end of 2026/27 and (£3,703k) at the end of 2030/31.
findings.detail: The forecast falls each year from 2026/27. The closing balance turns negative in 2029/30, and the paper records no funding solution for the gap in the figures shown.
findings.matters: A projected negative General Fund balance is the sort of trajectory a lender or peer finance officer would want to check against the council's own reserve policy.
findings.quote: General Fund Closing Balances 4,845 3,038 1,069 (1,286) (3,703)

findings.paper_title: MTFS and Business Strategy Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The 2025/26 General Fund revenue budget underspent by £2.5m, leaving a General Fund Reserve balance of £5.7m at 31 March 2026.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the underspend to a mix of underspends, additional income, budget carry forwards, changes in provisions, government grants and financial management. It is the starting point for the reserve forecasts in the MTFS.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size of a year-end underspend and the reserve it produced against their own position.
findings.figures: £2.5m underspend; £5.7m General Fund Reserve balance at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: There was an underspend of £2.5m on the General Fund revenue budget in 2025/26 resulting in a General Fund Reserve balance of £5.7m as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: The government's statutory override for pooled fund gains and losses has been extended to 1 April 2029
findings.detail: The override applies to pooled fund investments made before 1 April 2024 and keeps fair value movements out of the General Fund. The paper notes that current MHCLG communication suggests it will not be extended beyond 2029, and the council will discuss the implications with Arlingclose.
findings.matters: Pooled fund losses that are currently held in an unusable reserve would reach the General Fund if the override lapses, which would affect every council holding similar funds.
findings.figures: £8.0m in long-term investments across four funds; override extended to 1 April 2029
findings.quote: The override has been extended to 1 April 2029 for pooled fund investments made before 1 April 2024.

findings.headline: Interest receivable fell to £287k at an average rate of 3.97%, from £340k at 4.17% a year earlier
findings.detail: The paper says the fall is broadly in line with reductions in the Bank Rate. The average rate of 3.97% is compared with a SONIA average of 3.73% over the period.
findings.matters: Falling investment income reduces a council's revenue offset against its borrowing costs, which matters for any finance director managing the net financing position.
findings.figures: Interest receivable £287k at 3.97% (30/09/26); £340k at 4.17% (30/09/25); SONIA average 3.73%; Bank Rate 3.75%
findings.quote: The total interest receivable for the period ended 30 September 2026 amounted to £287k at an average rate of 3.97% (compared to £340k at 4.17% to 30 September 2025).

findings.headline: Most of the council's PWLB loans would carry a premium of between 5% and 99% on early repayment, and no rescheduling has taken place this year
findings.detail: The paper says some loans taken out in March 2012 at preferential rates would attract a smaller premium, and so have a higher chance of a discount if rates rise further. It states that no debt rescheduling has taken place in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Early-repayment premiums of this size limit a council's options to reduce debt costs, and the 2012 preferential loans show where a discount could arise.
findings.figures: Premium on premature repayment between 5% and 99% for most PWLB loans (as printed); average interest payable 3.75% at 30/09/26; average years to maturity 6.55 years
findings.quote: Currently most of the Council’s PWLB loans would attract a premium, i.e. a penalty, on premature repayment of between 5% and 99%.

findings.headline: Ten-year gilt yield rose from 4.86% to 5.43% over April to September 2026, which the paper says could make replacement loans dearer
findings.detail: The paper cites the rise in gilt yields and says that new loans could be more expensive than earlier funding. It notes that repaying an existing loan and replacing it may prove costly in the long term.
findings.matters: A council replacing maturing debt in the current market faces higher costs than it would have borne earlier, which bears on any early repayment or replacement decision across the sector.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt yield 4.86% at start of period, 5.43% at end; 20-year gilt yield 5.45% to 5.93%; PWLB standard rate 100 basis points above gilts
findings.quote: There is a risk that, as interest rates have risen dramatically recently, new loans could be more expensive and the initial decision to pursue the repayment of the original loan could turn out to be costly in the long term.

findings.headline: A £6.4m PWLB loan matures on 28 March 2027 and will need replacing, with £3.5m of EIP loans still to be repaid
findings.detail: A £1.5m PWLB loan was repaid in August 2026. The paper says the £6.4m loan will be replaced at least in part, depending on cash flows, with other borrowing before 31 March 2027. Of the EIP loans, £3.2m was repaid in the first half of the year and £3.5m remains due in the second half.
findings.matters: A maturing £6.4m PWLB loan and the replacement funding it requires show how a council is refinancing its debt within a single year.
findings.figures: £6.4m PWLB loan maturing 28 March 2027; £1.5m repaid August 2026; EIP loans £3.2m repaid, £3.5m remaining; PWLB short-term loans £14,333k at 01/04/26 and £9,890k at 30/09/26
findings.quote: One PWLB loan of £6.4m will mature on 28 March 2027.

findings.headline: Planned 2026/27 borrowing of £41m has not been fully taken out, with large investment balances covering the need so far
findings.detail: The paper says the borrowing required to fund the programme has not been fully undertaken because investment balances have meant no specific need arose. It adds that some borrowing may slip to 2027/28 if capital slippage continues.
findings.matters: A council deferring planned borrowing by running down investment balances is a choice a lender and a peer finance officer would track, since the borrowing will still be needed when balances fall.
findings.figures: £41m planned borrowing; £41.334m unfinanced capital expenditure; investments of £17.330m at 01/04/26 and £12.830m at 30/09/26
findings.quote: This borrowing has not yet been fully undertaken as the availability of large investment balances has meant that there has been no specific need to undertake this borrowing thus far.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital programme estimate has risen from £24,011k to £66,838k, with £20.6m of 2025/26 budgets brought forward
findings.detail: The paper attributes the change to the original estimate largely to unspent 2025/26 budgets brought forward, plus in-year changes and new schemes approved by Cabinet. A further £3.655m of schemes sit on a reserve list, excluded until a funding source is identified.
findings.matters: A near-threefold rise in the in-year capital estimate, funded in part by unfinanced expenditure and reserve-list items, drives the borrowing need a finance director must fund.
findings.figures: Original estimate £24,011k; estimate at 30/09/26 £66,838k; £20.6m brought forward from 2025/26; £21m of in-year approvals; reserve list £3.655m; unfinanced capital expenditure £41,334k
findings.quote: The change to the original estimate is largely due to bringing forward unspent capital budgets totalling £20.6m from 2025/26, in addition to several increases and reductions to various schemes and new schemes approved by Cabinet in year totalling £21m.

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The HRA Medium-Term Financial Strategy has not taken account of Local Government Reorganisation, and its projection period may run past the potential start date of a new unitary authority.
findings.detail: The paper says the MTFS end date may extend beyond the potential start date for any new unitary authority. It makes no allowance for the impact of LGR.
findings.matters: Any council in a reorganisation area needs to know whether its HRA projections extend beyond the point at which they could change hands.
findings.quote: has not taken any account of the impact of LGR

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The capital programme may be rescheduled, which could save revenue on prudential borrowing.
findings.detail: The paper says officers will review the timing of the replacement programme for compliance and affordability, and that some improvement works may be rescheduled or reprioritised.
findings.matters: Rescheduling capital spend to reduce prudential borrowing costs is a lever a finance director can compare with their own HRA capital plan.
findings.quote: for some revenue savings relating to prudential borrowing

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The paper cites lower than anticipated rent income in 2025/26 as one cause of the HRA working balance falling below £1 million.
findings.detail: The paper says the outturn resulted from rising costs accumulating over several years together with lower rent income than expected. It states that the working balance was affected by both.
findings.matters: A finance director can see rent income shortfall as a cause of an HRA reserve fall, separate from cost pressures.
findings.quote: lower than anticipated rent incomes being received in 2025/26

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The MTFS assumes a 4.5% rent uplift for 2027/28 and 3% thereafter, against a 4.8% social housing rent cap for 2026/27 with no government announcement yet for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper says the rent cap guidance may change and that the April 2026 guidance indicated the arrangement would run for 10 years. The MTFS shows a rent uplift of £1,000k in 2026/27 and £697k in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Rent uplift is the main income lever in the HRA, and a finance director can compare the assumed uplift with the government's stated cap.
findings.figures: 4.8% rent cap 2026/27; 4.5% assumed uplift 2027/28; 3% thereafter; £1,000k rent uplift 2026/27; £697k 2027/28
findings.quote: assumes a 4.5% uplift for 2027/28 and 3% thereafter

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The HRA MTFS assumes an average HRA borrowing rate of 4.5%, applied to maturing loans that will be rescheduled at current rates, with a £529k change in interest on borrowing in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper says the rate is based on existing prudential borrowing in the capital programme. It also says rising interest rates increase refinancing risk as significant loans from the 2012 Housing Finance Reforms mature.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, can compare an HRA refinancing assumption with its own and see how the 2012 reform debt is being handled.
findings.figures: 4.5% average HRA rate; £529k change in interest on borrowing 2026/27; £405k 2027/28

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The MTFS forecasts the HRA closing balance at £814k for 2026/27 and £1,097k for 2027/28, and says it is unlikely to return above £1 million in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper states that a more realistic target is to return above £1 million in 2027/28, to be firmed up at budget setting. The forecast balance then rises to £1,395k in 2028/29 and £2,083k in 2030/31.
findings.matters: It sets out a dated reserve recovery target, which a finance director can track against outturn as the forecast develops.
findings.figures: £814k closing 2026/27; £1,097k closing 2027/28; £2,083k closing 2030/31; £1 million minimum
findings.quote: it is unlikely that the HRA balance can be returned above £1 million in this financial year

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: There was a £276k overspend on the Housing Revenue Account budget, which increased the anticipated deficit on the HRA Working Balance.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the outturn to rising costs accumulating over several years and to lower than anticipated rent income in the year. It gives the year as "2025/56", which appears to be a typo for 2025/26.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare an HRA outturn overspend against revised estimates and see how it flowed into the working balance.
findings.figures: £276k overspend
findings.quote: There was a £276k overspend on the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) budget

findings.paper_title: HRA MTFS and Budget Action Plan Oct-26 FINAL
findings.headline: The HRA working balance stood at £946k at 31 March 2026, below the Section 151 Officer's £1 million minimum recommended level.
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA Working Balance dipped below the minimum recommended level, and that there is no specific statutory minimum, so a short-term dip can be tolerated. It says sustained efforts are needed to bring the balance back above £1 million.
findings.matters: It shows an HRA reserve falling below a s151 officer's recommended floor, with the council stating the position is tolerable only in the short term.
findings.figures: £946k at 31 March 2026; £1 million minimum recommended level
findings.quote: amounted to £946k as at 31 March 2026

findings.headline: Broxtowe's HRA budget needs £50k of efficiencies in 2026/27 and £300k in 2027/28 to return the working balance towards its £1 million minimum.
findings.detail: The paper says these efficiencies are needed to put the HRA Reserve on a more sustainable footing, and that the earlier they are found and secured, the better their medium-term impact. The MTFS table carries them as a Business Strategy line of (50) and (300).
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare how an HRA plans to close a reserve gap through specified annual efficiency targets, and whether they are yet identified.
findings.figures: £50k in 2026/27; £300k in 2027/28; minimum recommended balance £1 million
findings.quote: Budget efficiencies totalling £50k in 2026/27

findings.headline: Savills is reviewing 270 fire actions linked to wall construction, with results due by end October 2026
findings.detail: Savills is reviewing the 270 actions to confirm whether the external walls present no or limited risk, or to recommend further investigation. The report gives the end of October 2026 as the expected date for results.
findings.matters: External wall findings can lead to large remedial or investigation costs, so the outcome and its timing are relevant to any council carrying similar wall-construction exposure.
findings.figures: 270 wall-construction actions; results expected by end October 2026

findings.headline: 21 damp and mould cases were over 12 weeks old at September 2026, up 5 since the last report
findings.detail: The team is working to reduce cases over 12 weeks. The report gives access difficulties (10 cases) and decant requirements (6 cases) as the main reasons for delay.
findings.matters: Cases held up by decant and access problems tie completion timing to rehousing costs and legal action, which affects the cost of the programme.
findings.figures: 21 cases over 12 weeks; increase of 5 since the last report; 10 access issues; 6 decant required
findings.quote: (21 remaining, and increase of 5 since the last report)

findings.headline: Gas, LOLER and Legionella compliance were each reported at 100% for the period
findings.detail: The report records 100% compliance for gas servicing, lift inspections and legionella actions in the period. It states there are no concerns that the legionella deadlines will not be met.
findings.matters: Clean results across the statutory safety areas show where the programme is on track, which gives the board a contrast with the fire action and electrical backlogs.
findings.figures: Gas 100%; LOLER 100%; Legionella 100%; 372 gas services completed in the month
findings.quote: 100% compliance was achieved in this period.

findings.matters: The worst-case calculation shows the compliance figure would fall if inspections stop, and it depends on access that the council is trying to resolve through legal means.

findings.headline: Of 4,719 original Firntec fire risk actions, 3,879 are reported as meeting the desktop-review criteria, with 840 still being checked
findings.detail: A desktop exercise is reconciling the 2024 Firntec spreadsheet against the refreshed Savills FRAs to find out which original actions are completed, replicated or not required. findings.quote: Of the 4,719 original Firntec actions, the evidence gathered states that 3,879 meet the above criteria.

findings.headline: Procurement delays are holding up installation of lockable door sets, which make up over 50% of overdue FRA actions
findings.detail: The report says procurement processes have slowed the installation of lockable door sets. It records a lesson learned that future actions should be reviewed to decide whether procurement needs to start earlier.
findings.matters: Procurement lead time on remedial capital works is a timing risk that other councils with large fire safety programmes will also face.

findings.matters: The overdue count is the measure the board is tracking against remedial fire safety work, and a reader can see how quickly it moved in each direction over the year.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 3 Nov
findings.headline: The Housing and Asset Management restructure is on track to be completed in October 2026, centralising compliance oversight.
findings.detail: The restructure focuses on centralising compliance and strengthening oversight of Repairs and Damp and Mould. An early priority of the new compliance function is to commission an independent audit of fire and asbestos compliance.
findings.matters: It shows a dated organisational change tied to the regulator's requirements, and the planned independent audit may produce findings with cost consequences.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 3 Nov
findings.headline: Broxtowe reports no Housing Revenue Account financial implications at this stage, with any cost uplift beyond existing resources to require Cabinet approval.
findings.detail: The Deputy Chief Executive and Section 151 Officer state that the HRA has no financial implications to consider at this stage. Any future uplift in costs that cannot be met from existing resources would need Cabinet approval.
findings.matters: The council has not yet put a figure on the cost of the regulatory improvement plan, so any future HRA spending pressure would be decided through a new Cabinet approval rather than already provided for.
findings.quote: There are no financial implications to consider for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) at this stage.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 3 Nov
findings.headline: Outstanding fire safety actions rose by 190 to 1,981 after the annual reinspection of 26 Independent Living sites.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the increase to the cyclical annual reinspection of 26 Independent Living sites, with a further 16 re-inspections scheduled for the rest of the calendar year. The figure was shared with the Regulator on 23 October.
findings.matters: Remediation work on the open fire safety actions is not costed in the paper, so the financial effect of clearing the backlog is not yet visible to a finance reader.
findings.figures: 190 increase in outstanding fire safety actions; 1,981 total outstanding fire safety actions; 26 Independent Living sites; 16 further re-inspections
findings.quote: The number of actions has risen by 190 since the last report to a total of 1,981.

findings.headline: Fuel, light and water costs fell 15% to £112,500, generating £20,250 saving from new cremator installation and energy pricing
findings.detail: Fuel, light and water costs are forecast at £112,500 against a budget of £132,750, a saving of £20,250 or 15%. The paper attributes this to installation of new cremators, a better energy price scheme, and more efficient operation.
findings.matters: Demonstrates capital investment in new equipment generating measurable operational efficiency gains and validating the return on capital expenditure.
findings.figures: £112,500 projected; £132,750 budgeted; saving of £20,250 or 15%
findings.quote: Saving has been made due to the better price scheme, the installation of the new cremators and more efficient way of operation.

findings.headline: Business rates increased to £185,220 against budget of £155,600—a 19% cost overrun with no explanation
findings.detail: Business rates costs are forecast at £185,220, compared to a budget of £155,600, a variance of £29,620. The paper provides no explanation for this significant increase, which represents an uncontrollable external cost pressure.
findings.matters: Shows exposure to business rates inflation that significantly impacts operating margins in property-based services and lies outside management control.
findings.figures: £185,220 forecast; £155,600 budgeted; increase of £29,620 or 19%
findings.quote: Business rates higher than budgeted.

findings.headline: 'Your Cremation' service outperforming budget by 393% (projected £145,000 at-need income against £29,400 budget), plus £225,000 from prepaid packages
findings.detail: The 'Your Cremation' at-need service is forecast at £145,000 against a budget of £29,400, significantly exceeding expectations. Additional revenue of £225,000 from prepaid packages is held in earmarked reserve. The paper notes this success is offsetting the main cremation fee income decline.
findings.matters: Demonstrates successful revenue diversification strategy responding to core business decline, relevant for councils managing similar services under margin pressure.
findings.figures: £145,000 at-need income (vs £29,400 budgeted); £225,000 prepaid packages in reserve
findings.quote: the success of the 'Your Cremation' service and the figures do not include revenues generated from the prepaid packages which are held in an earmarked reserve

findings.headline: Cremation fee income declining 8.5% due to competitive markets and reduced death rate, creating structural revenue challenge
findings.detail: Cremation fee income is projected at £2,000,000 against a budget of £2,186,750 (a reduction of £186,750). The paper explicitly attributes this to competitive markets and lower death rates—both structural headwinds beyond management's direct control, combining pricing pressure with demographic decline.
findings.matters: Finance directors managing crematorium services need to understand these dual structural challenges and the consequent pressure to develop alternative revenue streams.
findings.figures: £2,000,000 projected; £2,186,750 budgeted; reduction of £186,750 or 8.5%
findings.quote: Less expected due to competitive markets and reduced death rate.

findings.headline: Budget pressure of £89,700 forecast for 2026/27, driven by reduced cremation fee income and increased operating costs, partially offset by 'Your Cremation' service
findings.detail: The crematorium is forecasting a net budget pressure of £89,700 from reduced cremation fee income (down £186,750 or 8.5%) and increased operating costs including business rates. This is partly offset by the 'Your Cremation' service generating £145,000 in at-need income plus £225,000 from prepaid packages held in earmarked reserve.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to track emerging pressures on joint committee services and understand whether management's diversification response can close the identified gap.
findings.figures: £89,700 pressure; cremation fee income £2,000,000 projected vs £2,186,750 budgeted; Your Cremation at-need £145,000; prepaid packages £225,000
findings.quote: The forecast position at this stage is a budget pressure of £89,700, from a net increase in operating costs and reduced cremation fee income. This is being offset by the success of the 'Your Cremation' service

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 29 Sept
findings.headline: Major restructure of Housing and Asset Management teams to centralize compliance scheduled for October 2026, one month after this meeting.
findings.detail: A restructure of Housing and Asset Management teams is underway to centralize compliance and strengthen oversight of key functions including repairs and damp and mold management. The restructure is in consultation stage and is scheduled to become operational in October 2026. This represents a significant organizational change following the regulatory judgment.
findings.matters: Major organizational restructuring shortly after a regulatory judgment indicates attempts to remediate compliance gaps but carries execution risk and potential cost implications that may not yet be quantified.
findings.figures: Scheduled for October 2026
findings.quote: The restructure within Housing and Asset Management teams, which focuses on centralising compliance and providing stronger oversight on key function such as Repairs and Damp and Mould, is in the consultation stage. It is envisaged that the restructure is operational by October 2026.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 29 Sept
findings.headline: Head of Legal Services warns council must implement Regulator's recommendations as soon as practicably possible or face formal consequences
findings.detail: The Head of Legal Services sets out the Regulator's formal powers under the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 and the Housing and Regeneration Act 2008, and emphasizes that failure to adhere will have consequences, requiring that recommendations be implemented 'as soon as practicably possible.'
findings.matters: Direct legal warning of consequences for non-compliance is a material risk signal regarding the council's ability to manage regulated services and comply with formal requirements.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Failure to adhere to the recommendations of the Regulator will have consequences.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 29 Sept
findings.headline: Section 151 Officer flags potential future Housing Revenue Account cost pressures despite no current financial implications.
findings.detail: The financial officer confirms there are no current financial implications for the Housing Revenue Account from the Service Improvement Plan. However, the officer explicitly warns that any future cost increases that cannot be absorbed within existing budgets would require Cabinet approval, indicating awareness that remediation could generate additional spending.
findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors need clarity on whether regulatory remediation will create budget pressures requiring additional funding or reserve draws.
findings.figures: None quantified
findings.quote: There are no financial implications to consider for the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) at this stage. Any uplift in costs going forward that cannot be contained within existing resources would require approval by Cabinet.

findings.paper_title: 1.0 RSH Housing Service Improvement Plan update 29 Sept
findings.headline: Council received C3 judgment from Regulator of Social Housing following October 2025 inspection.
findings.detail: Following an inspection in October 2025, the council received a C3 judgment from the Regulator of Social Housing. The council is implementing a refreshed Housing Service Improvement Plan addressing fire risk management, insight and inclusion, anti-social behavior, and complaints. A lessons learned exercise to identify root causes has been completed, and officers meet monthly with Regulator representatives.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance judgments indicate governance or operational deficiencies and could affect the council's creditworthiness and financial stability.
findings.figures: C3 judgment issued October 2025.
findings.quote: A lessons learned exercise, deigned to identify root causes for the C3 judgement has been completed.

findings.headline: General Fund capital contingency of £43,250 is being drawn down by multiple schemes, with pay-and-display car parks doubling from delayed spend
findings.detail: The car parks pay-and-display replacement scheme is doubling from £36,000 to £72,000 because work scheduled for 2025/26 was delayed and both phases are now happening in 2026/27. This, combined with other contingency draws (Toton Park and Ride £10,000), is depleting the remaining General Fund Capital Contingency balance of £43,250. The pay-and-display upgrade is necessary as current machines are end-of-life and risk critical.
findings.matters: Capital contingency is a buffer for unexpected costs and emergencies; rapid depletion limits the council's flexibility to respond to new capital pressures
findings.figures: Car parks budget revised £36,000 to £72,000; General Fund Capital Contingency balance £43,250 remaining; Toton Park and Ride £10,000 from contingency
findings.quote: There is currently a budget of £36,000 for this scheme in 2026/27 (carried forward from 2025/26), however it is expected that a total of £72,000 will be required this financial year as work planned for 2025/26 was delayed, so both phases of the work will take place in 2026/27. There is currently no budgetary provision for these additional works, so the uplift will be largely funded from the remaining balance of the General Fund Capital Contingency budget and be financed by prudential borrowing.

findings.headline: Council offices external works cost inflation of 53 per cent due to scaffolding price increases
findings.detail: Scaffolding costs have driven the Council Offices external works project to £115,000 from a £75,000 original budget—a £40,000 or 53 per cent increase. The works remain necessary to address maintenance issues, but the cost inflation reflects emerging construction cost pressures. The overage is being funded by virement from the Beeston Square Capital Works budget, which currently has no immediate calls on the funds.
findings.matters: Cost inflation on individual schemes signals emerging price pressures in the council's supply chains and construction costs
findings.figures: Original budget £75,000; revised budget £115,000; overage £40,000 (53% increase)
findings.quote: Since the initial budget submission, the cost of scaffolding has increased the total cost beyond the original budget of £75,000. The works are still required to address maintenance issues and ensure that the building is in good repair and condition. The cost of works is now quoted at up to £115,000.

findings.headline: Analogue phone line switch-off on 31 January 2027 forces £120,000 additional HRA borrowing for lifeline systems upgrade
findings.detail: The council's Independent Living schemes rely on analogue phone lines for speech call units and lifeline alarm systems serving vulnerable residents. The existing budget of £213,000 is insufficient to move all schemes to digital before the 31 January 2027 switch-off deadline, requiring an additional £120,000 of HRA prudential borrowing (with £50,000 funded from HRA Capital Contingency). The upgrade is essential to maintain continuity of service for residents.
findings.matters: An external deadline driven by telecoms infrastructure changes is forcing new borrowing and capital spend, with limited scope for savings or deferral
findings.figures: Additional £120,000 HRA prudential borrowing needed; original budget £213,000; £50,000 from HRA Capital Contingency
findings.quote: The analogue phone lines used for the speech call units and lifeline alarm system within the Council's Independent Living schemes will be switched off on 31 January 2027. This system is vital in ensuring the safety of vulnerable residents and it is imperative that the system is updated to digital before the switch off to ensure the continuity of service for residents.

findings.headline: Hemlock Gate housing scheme delivering a year ahead of schedule with early rental income for the HRA
findings.detail: The new build scheme at Hemlock Gate is progressing far faster than anticipated due to slowdown in the housing market prioritising the council's social housing units. The £1.838m budget from 2027/28 is being brought forward to 2026/27 to cover accelerated payments. The overall £9.366m scheme cost remains unchanged, with earlier delivery potentially reducing costs and generating vital rent income for the HRA sooner than expected.
findings.matters: Accelerated HRA rental income improves the council's financial position and cash flow, and early delivery of major schemes signals efficient capital management
findings.figures: £1.838m brought forward from 2027/28; overall scheme cost £9.366m unchanged; expected completion 2026/27 instead of later years
findings.quote: The rate of progress for the new build scheme at Hemlock Gate, off Coventry Lane ('Land at Bramcote Crematorium') has been far quicker than anticipated. Due to the slowdown in the housing market, the developer is prioritising the build of the Council's social housing units. This will result in the properties now being completed in 2026/27, far sooner than anticipated.

findings.headline: Pay award cost pressure of £67k if 3.3% uplift accepted against 3% budget assumption
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget assumed 3% pay inflation, but National Employers offered 3.3% on 2 June 2026. The offer remains unaccepted by unions. If accepted, the council quantifies the additional cost as 'around £67k' for the year.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted pay inflation is a direct hit to the bottom line with no mitigation identified; represents unfunded cost pressure.
findings.figures: £67k impact if 3.3% accepted; 0.3 percentage point difference from budgeted 3%
findings.quote: If this pay award is accepted later, the overall impact on the budget for the year would be around £67k.

findings.headline: Stapleford Towns Fund street improvement scheme flagged with explicit budget risk to completion
findings.detail: Early 2027 completion target with project designs underway and public consultation in September. The council explicitly notes that 'budget remains a risk until completion,' suggesting the full scope or timeline could drive costs above the allocated budget within the multi-year scheme.
findings.matters: Acknowledged budget risk on externally-funded scheme affects council's ability to deliver town regeneration commitments within available funding.
findings.figures: Part of Stapleford Towns Fund (£5.713m approved), target completion early 2027
findings.quote: Project to complete early 2027, although budget remains a risk until completion.

findings.headline: Housing structural repairs budget at 28% spend in Q1 (£56k of £200k), with flagged risk due to case numbers and legacy issues
findings.detail: At 28% spend in Q1 (£56k of £200k), the council flags 'some risk with budget due to number of cases and legacy issues.' Legacy property defects are harder to predict and potentially cost more than anticipated.
findings.matters: Structural defects are not discretionary spending; unbudgeted costs cannot be deferred and may force reductions elsewhere.
findings.figures: £200k budget, £56k spent to 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Structural Remedial Repairs: 200 56 In progress. Some risk with budget due to number of cases and legacy issues.

findings.headline: Housing damp proofing programme 50% spent by end of Q1 with acknowledged budget risk
findings.detail: The damp proofing works have consumed £75k of a £150k annual budget in just three months, with the council noting risk 'with half of budget already spent.' This pace of spending suggests potential year-end budget exhaustion.
findings.matters: Rapid budget consumption in Q1 signals potential underfunding of housing condition works, requiring scope reduction or additional allocation mid-year.
findings.figures: £150k budget, £75k spent (50%), within first three months of financial year
findings.quote: Damp Proofing Works: 150 75 In progress. Some risks with half of budget already spent.

findings.headline: Brinsley Headstocks refurbishment costs flagged as likely to exceed £137k budget
findings.detail: The procurement stage for this scheme is in its final stage, with the council explicitly noting that costs are likely to exceed the approved budget. No spend has yet occurred in Q1.
findings.matters: Cost overruns on approved capital schemes require finding additional funding or cutting other priorities, affecting overall capital delivery.
findings.figures: £137k budget, £0 spent to 30 June 2026
findings.quote: Refurbishment of Brinsley Headstocks: 137 - Final stage of procurement underway, costs are likely to exceed budget.

findings.paper_title: Statement of Accounts Update and Outturn Position 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA deficit driven by both rising costs and falling rent income, with no immediate recovery plan detailed
findings.detail: The paper attributes the HRA deterioration to 'an accumulation of rising costs over several years and lower than anticipated rent incomes being received in 2025/26'. An HRA Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Business Strategy is being developed to address this, but the paper does not detail specific interventions or timescales.
findings.matters: Sustained cost inflation combined with income below forecast suggests the HRA model is under structural pressure, not just a one-year variance. Without visible recovery steps, the trend is concerning.
findings.figures: HRA overspend £276k; working balance deficit £946k
findings.quote: This outturn position has resulted from an accumulation of rising costs over several years and lower than anticipated rent incomes being received in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Statement of Accounts Update and Outturn Position 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA Working Balance has fallen below the Section 151 Officer's minimum recommended level of £1 million
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account working balance stood at £946k as at 31 March 2026, below the £1m minimum. This follows a £276k overspend against revised estimates, driven by accumulating rising costs and lower-than-anticipated rent income in 2025/26. The council acknowledges this can be tolerated short-term but says sustained efforts are required to recover.
findings.matters: A working balance below minimum signals tightening cash flexibility and suggests the council is managing HRA pressures through reserve depletion rather than service adjustment or rent increases. For lenders, this indicates housing finances are under strain.
findings.figures: HRA Working Balance £946k as at 31 March 2026; minimum recommended level £1m; HRA overspend £276k against revised estimates
findings.quote: With the budget deficit being higher than anticipated, the HRA Working Balance has now dipped below the Section 151 Officer's minimum recommended level of £1 million.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Audit of Accounts and Associated Matters
findings.headline: Regulator of Social Housing issued C3 grade in January 2026, citing serious failings in consumer standards
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing assigned a C3 rating to Broxtowe citing serious failings in delivering consumer standards outcomes, with significant improvements required. The auditor has identified this as a risk indicating a significant weakness in the council's arrangements for the 2025-26 financial year.
findings.matters: A C3 regulatory rating signals governance and operational failures in the council's social housing management, raising material concerns about management capability and service delivery effectiveness.
findings.figures: C3 grade issued January 2026
findings.quote: In January 2026, The Regulator of Social Housing issued a C3 grade for the Council, citing serious failings in the delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvements were needed.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates structural uncertainty with ongoing Government participation required
findings.detail: The council is participating in Government-directed Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) process. An internal LGR Implementation Group meets fortnightly and a dedicated reorganisation specialist officer has been appointed. The council is preparing for potential structural change but the outcome and timeline remain uncertain.
findings.matters: LGR represents fundamental uncertainty about the council's future structure, functions, funding arrangements, and viability; lenders must understand transition risks, potential effects on service continuity, and long-term ability to service debt.
findings.figures: 1 reorganisation specialist officer appointed; implementation group meets fortnightly
findings.quote: There is an internal Local Government Reorganisation Implementation Group that meets fortnightly and an Officer has been appointed as the Council's Reorganisation specialist.

findings.headline: Budget gap identified requiring financial strategy refresh and cost reduction actions
findings.detail: The council reviewed and refreshed its Medium-Term Financial Strategy and Business Strategy in November 2025 in response to identified financial challenges. The refreshed Business Strategy sets out required actions to reduce costs, generate additional income, and improve services. A forward-looking action plan includes another MTFS review with a target date of November 2026 to ensure the budget gap is managed at a sustainable level.
findings.matters: Budget gaps directly threaten financial sustainability and debt service capacity; a lender needs confidence that identified shortfalls have credible, fully-costed solutions—the timing (still working on it six months into the year) raises questions about execution.
findings.figures: Budget gap identified November 2025; gap management plan due November 2026
findings.quote: The Business Strategy identified the actions required to reduce costs, generate additional income and/or improve services in order to meet the financial challenges faced by the Council and to mitigate against any budget risks.

findings.headline: Chief Executive retired mid-year; interim leadership appointed while permanent recruitment underway
findings.detail: The council's long-standing Chief Executive retired during 2025/26. The council appointed an Interim Chief Executive, Interim Deputy Chief Executive, and three additional interim director-level appointments to maintain resilience. Permanent recruitment for the Chief Executive is in progress but not yet complete as of the governance statement date (May 2026).
findings.matters: Leadership continuity is critical during periods of financial stress and regulatory challenge; interim arrangements create governance and execution risks, particularly given the council is simultaneously addressing a budget gap and a housing regulator failure.
findings.figures: 1 chief executive retired; 4 interim senior positions created (1 chief executive, 1 deputy, 3 directors)
findings.quote: During 2025/26 the Council's long-standing Chief Executive retired. Full Council appointed an Interim Chief Executive and an Interim Deputy Chief Executive while the permanent recruitment process takes place.

findings.headline: Housing regulator inspection resulted in C3 rating with serious failings in fire safety and tenant needs
findings.detail: The Regulator of Social Housing completed an inspection in October 2025 and rated Broxtowe C3, the worst rating under new assessment regulations introduced in 2023. The inspection identified two serious failings: fire safety management (unclear timelines on open actions, no evidence of mitigations in place), and inability to understand and tailor services to diverse tenant groups. The council is implementing a Service Improvement Plan to address these.
findings.matters: Regulatory failure in a core housing service indicates operational and compliance weaknesses, exposes the council to reputational damage and remediation costs, and reflects governance gaps that could affect creditworthiness and lender confidence.
findings.figures: C3 rating; serious failings identified in 2 areas (fire safety, diverse needs); weaknesses also identified in data quality, performance reporting, complaints learning, and ASB/hate crime accessibility
findings.quote: Following the inspection, Broxtowe Borough Council has received a C3 rating from RSH, meaning that the Council is not meeting the Regulator's requirements and must work to improve its position.

findings.headline: Non-compliance with Regulator recommendations will carry formal consequences, with implementation required as soon as practicable
findings.detail: The Head of Legal Services explicitly states that failure to adhere to the Regulator's recommendations will have consequences and emphasizes that implementation must occur as soon as practicably possible. This indicates active regulatory enforcement powers beyond the improvement plan itself.
findings.matters: This signals that non-compliance with the improvement plan carries formal regulatory penalties, making the compliance deadline material and urgent
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Failure to adhere to the recommendations of the Regulator will have consequences. It is imperative that the Regulators recommendations are considered and implemented as soon as practicably possible.

findings.headline: The council faces potential future compliance costs from the Regulator's requirements, with scale unknown and requiring cabinet approval if they exceed current resources
findings.detail: The Section 151 Officer confirms there are currently no financial implications to the Housing Revenue Account from the C3 rating. However, the statement explicitly reserves that any future cost uplift from compliance work that cannot be absorbed within existing resources will require Cabinet approval, indicating potential financial exposure.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need visibility of potential costs from regulatory compliance, even if currently unquantified, as they could affect HRA budget flexibility
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: There are no financial implications to consider for the Housing Revenue Account at this stage. Any uplift in costs going forward that cannot be contained within existing resources would require approval by Cabinet.

findings.headline: Broxtowe received C3 rating from Regulator of Social Housing following October 2025 inspection
findings.detail: Following an inspection in October 2025, the first assessment under the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023, Broxtowe received a C3 rating from RSH. This means the council is not meeting regulatory requirements and must work to improve. The Regulator noted constructive engagement but made clear that improvement is required.
findings.matters: A regulatory failure is a material governance issue that signals potential systemic problems in housing service delivery and could affect the council's standing as a regulated provider
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Following the inspection, the Council has received a C3 rating from RSH, meaning that the Council is not meeting the Regulator's requirements and must work to improve its position.

findings.headline: Pension fund currently fully funded at 105% with employer contributions at 16.8%, next actuarial valuation in March 2028 will set rates for 2029/30
findings.detail: The pension fund is currently fully funded at 105% and employer contributions have reduced to 16.8% of salary. However, the next actuarial valuation (March 2028) will set new contribution rates for 2029/30—precisely when the council's reserves are forecast to be critically depleted.
findings.matters: Any increase in pension contributions directly reduces available budget. A valuation change requiring higher contributions would hit the council at the moment it has minimal reserves to absorb the cost.
findings.figures: Current employer primary contribution 16.8% (down from 19.0%); next valuation March 2028 for 2029/30 implementation
findings.quote: The Pension Fund continues to perform well, with the Broxtowe element now fully funded at 105%. This may change again at the next actuarial valuation in March 2028 which will identify the employer's pension contributions required from 2029/30.

findings.headline: Capital receipts assumed in MTFS financing; £3.0m prudential borrowing proposed 2026/27 if receipts do not materialise
findings.detail: The MTFS financing depends on assumed capital receipts (from asset sales). The document warns that if these do not materialise, the council will need to fund infrastructure from other resources or borrowing, with potential 'significant impact on the viability of the MTFS'.
findings.matters: Capital receipts are volatile and dependent on market conditions; if assets cannot be sold as forecast, either capital schemes are delayed (reducing service resilience) or the council increases borrowing (reducing financial flexibility).
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing of £3.0m proposed for 2026/27; no quantified capital receipts target disclosed
findings.quote: Should anticipated capital receipts not materialise, the Council will need to fund its infrastructure, including any new construction projects, fleet vehicles, maintenance and development of ICT systems and key assets, from other resources. This may have a significant impact on the viability of the MTFS.

findings.headline: Annual revenue deficits accelerate from £760k to £2.28m over the MTFS period, widening the structural imbalance
findings.detail: The council's annual deficits—the gap between budgeted expenditure and available income—grow substantially and persistently from 2026/27 onwards. By 2029/30 the annual deficit has tripled, indicating the Business Strategy frontloads easier savings while future years require progressively larger interventions.
findings.matters: Accelerating deficits indicate an unsustainable trajectory; the widening gap suggests the council cannot close the structural funding gap with current policy.
findings.quote: PLANNED (SURPLUS)/DEFICIT AFTER MOVEMENT IN RESERVES TO BE FUNDED FROM GENERAL FUND BALANCE: 760 / 1,246 / 1,908 / 2,280

findings.headline: Leisure facilities are reaching end-of-life and creating increasing capital budget pressure, with strategy review underway
findings.detail: The council's leisure facilities, managed through Liberty Leisure Limited, are ageing and placing 'increasing pressures on capital budgets'. The council is currently reviewing its Leisure Facilities Strategy to determine the way forward.
findings.matters: Aging leisure infrastructure typically requires substantial capital expenditure to replace or refurbish; timing and cost of these decisions will materially affect capital programme and borrowing needs.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: Further challenges exist as the facilities through which leisure service operates are reaching the end-of-life stage and are placing increasing pressures on capital budgets. The Council is reviewing its Leisure Facilities Strategy, in order to develop a way forward for leisure services provision across Broxtowe.

findings.headline: Central government funding faces high risk from Fair Funding Review and Business Rates reset; outstanding rates appeals create further uncertainty
findings.detail: The council's funding is highly exposed to the Fair Funding Review outcome and Business Rates Retention Scheme reset. Outstanding rates appeals by businesses create material but unquantifiable uncertainty: the council acknowledges it is 'a challenge to come up with a meaningful estimate as to the level of rate reductions'.
findings.matters: Government funding and business rates are core income; volatility in these sources directly affects ability to balance without further reserve drawdown, and the council cannot control or predict outcomes.
findings.figures: Business Rates Baseline Funding Level drops from £4.610m (2025/26) to £2.995m (2026/27); Revenue Support Grant drops from £4.791m (2026/27) to £3.4m (2027/28 onwards)
findings.quote: The re-set of the Business Rates Retention Scheme has highlighted risks and vulnerability that local authorities face for reasons which are outside of their control.

findings.headline: Council budget balance depends on Business Strategy proposals "still being developed and finalised and may carry some implementation risk
findings.detail: The council's budget balance depends entirely on unfinalized Business Strategy proposals. The document explicitly states these proposals are 'still being developed and finalised and may carry some implementation risk'. Without these, the council falls into negative reserves.
findings.matters: Implementation risk on core savings means the MTFS is contingent on uncertain delivery; a lender must understand which savings are firm versus speculative.
findings.figures: Not quantified by proposal; aggregate delivered into base budget figures
findings.quote: Members will be aware that some savings or income proposals are still being developed and finalised and may carry some implementation risk which could have an impact on the savings or income profile. It is essential for the financial health of the Council over the medium term that these efficiencies and additional income are achieved.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves fall to zero by 2029/30 on current trajectory, leaving no contingency buffer
findings.detail: The council's General Fund reserves are forecast to decline from £4.215m (March 2026) to £300k by end of 2028/29, then into negative territory (-£1.979m) in 2029/30. The council's s151 officer advises minimum reserves should be £1.5m; available reserves therefore drop to -£1.2m in 2028/29 and -£3.479m in 2029/30.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty the council can weather unexpected events; reserves at these levels indicate the council is structurally insolvent unless all savings execute perfectly.
findings.figures: Opening £4.215m; closing 2028/29 £300k; closing 2029/30 -£1,979k. Minimum advised £1.5m. Available reserves 2028/29 -£1,200k; 2029/30 -£3,479k.
findings.quote: If all the assumptions as set out in this MTFS arise, and no further action is taken with regards to Business Strategy proposals, then overall reserve levels will reduce to just £300k by the end of 2028/29 and the fall into a negative position during 2029/30 and beyond.

findings.headline: Annual Bramcote Crematorium distribution to Broxtowe budgeted at £450k for 2026/27, conditional on meeting 2025/26 performance targets
findings.detail: The council receives an annual distribution from its joint ownership of Bramcote Crematorium with Erewash Borough Council. The 2026/27 distribution is budgeted at £450k. However, the strategy explicitly warns that 'any failure by the Crematorium to meet its targets for 2025/26 will be reflected in the distribution for 2026/27,' flagging income volatility tied to operational performance.
findings.matters: A £450k income stream is meaningful; the explicit performance caveat signals that budgeted income may not materialise if crematorium operations falter
findings.figures: Distribution to Broxtowe 2026/27: £450k
findings.quote: Any failure by the Crematorium to meet its targets for 2025/26 will be reflected in the distribution for 2026/27.

findings.headline: Investment income forecast to fall 55% from £997k to £450k as cash balances and rates decline
findings.detail: The council forecasts investment interest income (less costs) will drop from £997k in 2024/25 to £450k in 2026/27. This reflects both lower interest rates and the drawdown of the investment base. The weighted average investment balance is forecast to fall from £21,580k to £13,000k. This materially reduces non-service revenue available to support council operations.
findings.matters: A 55% reduction in investment income is a significant loss of discretionary revenue; combined with reserve drawdown, it signals tighter financial flexibility
findings.figures: Total Interest 2024/25: £997k; Total Interest 2026/27: £450k; Weighted Average Total Investments 2024/25: £21,580k; 2026/27: £13,000k

findings.headline: Investment balances forecast to fall from £21,151k to £12,000k by March 2027, then £10,000k by March 2028, as regeneration capital schemes near completion
findings.detail: Total investment exposure is forecast to drop from £21,151k at 31 March 2026 to £12,000k at 31 March 2027, then plateau at £10,000k. The council explicitly attributes this to 'large capital grant funded regeneration schemes nearing completion and therefore the cash balances held for these schemes being fully applied.' This represents a one-time event that permanently reduces the council's liquidity buffer by roughly half.
findings.matters: Lenders assess financial strength through cash reserves; this signals lower financial headroom from 2027/28 onwards to cover unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls
findings.figures: Investments 1 April 2025: £21,151k; Investments 31 March 2027: £12,000k; Investments 31 March 2028–2029: £10,000k
